prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: roof tiles blown off in a storm. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 3)
response: {"items":[{"type":"fact","content":"When a storm has lifted roof tiles, the claim is usually straightforward if the photos show matching wind damage across the roofline and there is no sign of long-term wear or slipping from age."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the damage is limited to a few missing tiles, I should still check for hidden water ingress, because small breaches can lead to larger internal loss than the roof damage itself suggests."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the insured has kept spare tiles or the roof uses a common profile, temporary make-safe and like-for-like repair are often within delegated authority and can be arranged quickly."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the tiles are brittle, mismatched or obsolete, I should expect a repair to become more complex, as colour and profile matching can matter as much as the physical fixing work."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the storm also damaged ridge or hip tiles, I should treat those separately from loose main tiles, because the repair method and urgency can differ."},{"type":"observation","content":"When photographs are taken from ground level only, I may need extra evidence or a surveyor view, because detached tiles can be obvious while the extent of surrounding uplift is easy to miss."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the weather event is clear from Met Office records and the loss description is consistent, I prefer to move quickly to make-safe rather than wait for every technical question to be answered."},{"type":"fact","content":"When tarpaulin or emergency covering is in place, I should confirm whether it was fitted promptly and properly, because that often limits any resulting escape of water and shows sensible mitigation."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the roof is already near the end of its life, I should look carefully for wear, missing bedding mortar and prior patching, because storm may have exposed an existing maintenance problem rather than caused the whole issue."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the claim is only for blown-off tiles with no internal damage, I can usually keep the assessment simple: verify storm, confirm the damaged section, and authorise a proportionate repair within limits."}]}
